syllabusTopics: Hydrogen: chemistry of atomic and nascent hydrogen; isotopes of hydrogen and their uses
Application of hydrogen as fuel; heavy water and its applications
Allotropes of oxygen: definition of allotropy and examples; oxygen — types of oxides (acidic, basic, neutral, amphoteric, peroxide and mixed oxides)
Applications of hydrogen peroxide; medical and industrial application of oxygen
Ozone: occurrence, preparation of ozone from oxygen, structure of ozone, test for ozone, uses of ozone
Ozone layer depletion: causes, effects and control measures

Halogens: general characteristics of halogens; comparative study on preparation, chemical properties (with water, alkali, ammonia, oxidizing character, bleaching action) and uses of Cl2, Br2 and I2
Test for Cl2, Br2 and I2

rows.label: Concept
rows.text: Phosphorus wears three structural masks. **White P** — waxy, discrete P₄ tetrahedra whose 60° angles strain every bond — ignites at 35 °C, glows in the dark, dissolves in CS₂, poisons at 0.1 g, and lives under water; it fed the old strike-anywhere matches, rat poisons and smoke screens.…

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: "White phosphorus is a waxy, poisonous solid of P4 tetrahedra that ignites spontaneously in air; red phosphorus is its safe, polymeric counterpart."

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: ***The underwater knife*** - white phosphorus is cut under water: in air the friction of the blade would ignite it; the water is both shield and solvent of heat.

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: White: P4, 60 deg strain, ignites 35 C, under water, CS2-soluble, poisonous, glows. Red: polymer, 250-300 C conversion, safe, matchbox side. Black: layered, most stable, semiconductor. Reverse: distil red > 400 C.

rows.text: **NEB-style (3m): Name the allotropes of phosphorus and compare white and red phosphorus in structure, reactivity and uses.** — **Allotropes:** white (yellow), red and black phosphorus. **White phosphorus:** discrete **P₄ tetrahedra** with bond angles strained to 60°; consequently extremely reactive — it ignites spontaneously in air at…  ·  **NEB-style (2m): Why is white phosphorus kept under water, and what happens when red phosphorus is distilled above 400 °C?** — White phosphorus ignites in air at about 35 °C because its P₄ tetrahedra carry severe bond-angle strain; it is stored (and cut) **under water** to exclude air — water also does not dissolve it.…

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: Strain is reactivity: the P4 tetrahedron forces 60-degree bonds onto atoms wanting ~100 degrees, so white phosphorus burns at 35 C while red phosphorus - the same atoms with the strain polymerised away - sits safely in a matchbox striking surface.

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: Phosphorus allotropes (names only per NEB): WHITE (yellow) P - waxy, discrete P4 tetrahedra with strained 60 deg angles, ignites ~35 C, stored under water, soluble in CS2, very poisonous (~0.1 g), garlic odour, glows in dark (chemiluminescence from slow oxidation); uses old matches, rat poison, smoke screens.…

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: Phosphorus means "light-bearer": the element was named for the cold glow of its slow oxidation, noticed centuries before the structure was known.

rows.label: More practice
rows.text: **NEB-style (2m): Explain why red phosphorus is used on the side of a safety-match box while white phosphorus was used in old strike-anywhere matches.** — **Safety match:** the box side carries **red phosphorus**; the stick head carries the oxidant (**KClO₃**) with antimony sulphide and glue.…

Scientific Definitions | Term | Scientific meaning | Example | |---|---|---| | **Allotropy** | Same element, different structural forms | white/red/black P | | **P₄ tetrahedron** | Four P atoms at tetrahedral corners, 60° P–P–P | white phosphorus | | **Chemiluminescence** | Light from a chemical reaction | white P glow | | **Spontaneous ignition** | Ignition at ambient…  ·  ## 4. Detailed Explanation ### 4.1 Why white phosphorus is so reactive - The P₄ tetrahedron forces 60° angles on atoms whose bonding orbitals prefer ~90–109° — the bent bonds are strained, energy-rich, and desperate to react. Ignition at 35 °C follows; hence storage under water (cutting it under water too — it ignites on the knife).…  ·  ## 5.
